title: Gravity and Mass
seo_title: Grade 8 Gravity Worksheets: Mass, Weight, Distance and Gravitational Attraction
standard_text: Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on gravity (NGSS MS-PS2-4): gravity as an attractive force, how mass and distance affect it, mass vs. weight, and weight on the Moon and other planets. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Gravity always pulls, and more mass pulls harder.
key_sub: Gravitational force grows with mass and shrinks with distance. Weight changes from world to world; mass does not.
body_html:
How to think about it

Gravity is a force of attraction between any two objects with mass. It never pushes.

  • More mass → stronger gravity. The Sun pulls harder than Earth; Earth pulls harder than the Moon.
  • More distance → weaker gravity.
  • The two objects pull on each other with equal forces.

Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. Weight (N) is the pull of gravity and changes: on the Moon you weigh about 1/6 as much.

Example

You weigh 540 N on Earth. What do you weigh on the Moon?

540 ÷ 6

Answer: 90 N

Example

Your mass is 50 kg on Earth. What is it on Mars?

Mass does not change.

Answer: 50 kg

Common mistakes

  • Thinking there is no gravity in space.
  • Thinking mass changes on other planets. Only weight changes.
  • Thinking gravity can push objects away.

faq.q: What does the strength of gravity depend on?
faq.a: The masses of the two objects and the distance between them. More mass makes it stronger; more distance makes it weaker.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass and changes on other planets.

faq.q: Why do astronauts float in the space station?
faq.a: They and the station are falling around Earth together. Gravity is still pulling on them.

items.q: Why does the Sun have the strongest gravity in the solar system?
c: It has by far the most mass.
items.e: Mass determines gravity.

items.q: Leo asks about the gravitational force between the Sun and Jupiter. Which statement is correct?
c: The Sun pushes the other away.
There is no force between them.
They pull on each other with forces of equal size.
items.e: Gravity is a pair of attractive forces (Newton's third law).

items.q: Luis compares a bowling ball and a marble. Which has a stronger gravitational pull on objects near it at the same distance?
c: A bowling ball, because it has more mass.
A marble, because it has less mass.
items.e: More mass means stronger gravity.

items.q: Eli observes: “Ocean tides rise and fall twice a day.” Which explanation is best supported by evidence?
c: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans.
items.e: Gravity is an attractive force between all masses.

items.q: Kai observes: “Ocean tides rise and fall twice a day.” Which explanation is best supported by evidence?

items.e: Gravity is an attractive force between all masses.

items.q: Is there gravity in space?
c: Yes. Gravity reaches far into space and holds planets in orbit.
items.e: Gravity weakens with distance but never stops.

items.q: What happens to the gravitational force if two objects move farther apart?
items.e: Distance weakens gravity.

items.q: Why do you weigh less on the Moon?
c: The Moon is made of air.
The Moon has less mass than Earth, so its gravity is weaker.
items.e: Less mass → weaker pull.
